newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian police prevent opposition demo.
newsitem.headline: Albanian police prevent opposition demo.

text.p: Albanian police manhandled and beat demonstrators in the capital on Saturday to prevent opposition parties from holding a rally against President Sali Berisha and the collapse of pyramid investment schemes.

But tens of thousands of people, chanting anti-government slogans, massed for a fourth day in the southern port of Vlore. Protesters also took to the streets of another southern town, Fier, before being dispersed by police.

Tirana police, some with riot gear, pushed people down side streets away from the main Skanderbeg Square, where the banned rally was to have taken place. They used truncheons on anyone objecting or failing to move away quickly enough.
About 500 marchers were dispersed about one km (600 yards) from the huge square, left eerily deserted in early afternoon.
Three leaders of the opposition Socialist Party were bundled into a car and driven away.
"The police beat me up. I'm still covered in blood," prominent Socialist Kastriot Islami said by telephone after being released from a police station. "I don't know what happened to my colleagues."

The Interior Ministry denied any opposition figures had been arrested. It said in a statement that police had "taken under protection opposition leaders...summoned by Tirana police chiefs and told such actions were illegal. They were then escorted to (party) headquarters".
A Socialist Party spokesman said 15 party leaders were detained but later released.

A demonstration in favour of Berisha's Democratic Party was allowed to proceed unhindered close to the main square, with some 300 government supporters gathering in front of the Party's unfinished headquarters.
"We belong to civilised Europe," one banner read. A dozen cars raced down central boulevards, horns blaring and Democratic Party flags fluttering from the windows.
Many journalists scrambling to cover the failed rally had their equipment smashed or confiscated. Some were badly beaten.
Three men identifying themselves as members of "special security forces" entered Reuters Tirana bureau and demanded pictures and television film before being asked to leave.
In Vlore, up to 40,000 people took to the streets demanding the return of their life savings swallowed by the collapsed pyramid schemes. It was the largest protest this week.
Further north in Fier, about 2,000 demonstrators massed near the city main square. But police broke up the rally, attacking protesters and journalists with wooden sticks.
The protests were a resumption of widespread riots which swept Albania last month in an initial upsurge of anger against the collapsing pyramid schemes.
A swift police crackdown and a string of arrests following January's disturbances seemed to deter people from holding further protests for a time.
The Democratic Party, in a statement broadcast on state television, warned Albanians against what it termed "the red terror" being organised by the main opposition Socialist Party.
"The Democratic Party calls on all citizens not to blindly follow forces aiming to create a drama many times worse than that of the pyramid schemes," it said.

The Democrats won re-election last year in polls criticised as unfair by Western observers. Some opposition politicians accuse the party of financing the victory with proceeds from the failed pyramid companies.
